title: Fewest Edits Between Words
statement:
You get two strings a and b. One edit changes a in one of three ways:

  • insert one character anywhere,
  • delete one character,
  • replace one character with a different one.

Return the smallest number of edits that turns a into b.

examples.why: Delete the f, then add an n at the end. Comparing position by position finds 4 mismatches, because every letter is shifted by one.
From an empty string, the only way is to insert all 3 letters.
There is no "swap" edit, so exchanging the a and the m costs 2: two replacements, or a delete plus an insert.

constraints: a and b hold lowercase English letters
hints: Look only at the last character of each string. If they are equal, do they need any edit? If not, what could the last edit that fixes the end of the string have been?
Let dp[i][j] be the fewest edits that turn a[0..i) into b[0..j). Turning a prefix into the empty string, or the empty string into a prefix, costs its length.

Equal last characters: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]. Otherwise 1 + min(dp[i−1][j−1] (replace), dp[i−1][j] (delete a[i−1]), dp[i][j−1] (insert b[j−1])). Each cell needs the cell above, the cell to the left and the diagonal, so keep one row plus one saved diagonal value.

explain.intuition:
Let dp[i][j] be the fewest edits that turn the first i characters of a into the first j characters of b. Focus on the end of both prefixes and ask what the last move did to make them line up.

If a[i−1] == b[j−1], the ends already agree, so leave them and solve the rest: dp[i−1][j−1]. Otherwise one of three moves fixes the end. Replace a[i−1] with b[j−1]: both ends are used, 1 + dp[i−1][j−1] (the diagonal). Delete a[i−1]: a's prefix shrinks, 1 + dp[i−1][j] (the cell above). Insert b[j−1] at the end: b's last character is now matched, 1 + dp[i][j−1] (the cell to the left). Take the cheapest. The edges are the easy cases: dp[i][0] = i deletes and dp[0][j] = j inserts. This is the same table a spell checker or a fuzzy search box uses to rank "did you mean" suggestions.
steps: Let row[j] = j for j = 0..m: turning an empty prefix of a into b[0..j).
For each i from 1 to n: save diag = row[0] (the old top-left), then set row[0] = i.
For each j from 1 to m: keep up = row[j]. If the characters match, row[j] = diag; else row[j] = 1 + min(diag, up, row[j−1]). Then set diag = up for the next column.
pitfalls: Comparing position by position, or only counting characters that differ. A single insert or delete shifts everything after it, as in the first example.
Paying 1 even when the last characters match. A match is free: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1].
In the one-row version, reading the diagonal from row[j−1]. By then it holds the new row's value; the old one must be saved before it is overwritten.

solutions.title: Recursion over the three moves
solutions.idea: Compare from the front: skip matching characters, otherwise try replace, delete and insert and take the cheapest. Without memory the three branches repeat the same subproblems.

solutions.title: Table over both prefixes
solutions.idea: dp[i][j] from the diagonal (match or replace), the cell above (delete) and the cell to the left (insert). Edges are i deletes and j inserts.

solutions.title: One row and a saved diagonal
solutions.idea: row[j] before the update is the cell above, row[j − 1] after its update is the cell to the left, and the diagonal is the old row[j − 1], saved in a variable.

followups: Return the actual list of edits, not just the count. How do you walk back through the table?
Insert and delete cost 1 but replace costs 2. What changes, and how does the answer relate to the longest shared subsequence?
You only care whether the distance is at most k, for a small k. Which cells of the table can you skip?
